AGENT-Pedagogical-Audit-Principles.title: AGENT-Pedagogical-Audit-Principles
AGENT-Pedagogical-Audit-Principles.content:
Pedagogical Audit Principles
Purpose
Every page of Learn to Read French / Learn to Read Proust must be auditable.
A chapter is not accepted because it sounds elegant.
It is accepted only if it has a clear learning target, a reliable pedagogical source, a visible reading action, card-conversion potential, and self-testing value.
Source Traditions
The textbook draws from five traditions:

Reading-knowledge French textbooks
Classical-language reading textbooks
Instructed second language acquisition
Input processing and form-meaning mapping
Retrieval practice through cards and diagnostic feedback

Reading-Knowledge French Textbook Tradition
Examples:

French for Reading
A Short Course in Reading French
French for Reading Knowledge courses

Principles:

begin with cognates and recognition
introduce false friends early
teach word families
prioritize function words
teach reading grammar, not conversation-first French

Classical-Language Reading Textbook Tradition
Examples:

Learn to Read Latin
Learn to Read Greek

Principles:

morphology and syntax must be explicit
literary target text motivates the sequence
early forms and grammar prepare for later difficult texts
reading goal is central

Instructed SLA
Principles:

instruction must have clear learning targets
learner performance must be observable
no single theory is sufficient
chapters must be revised from evidence

Input Processing
Principles:

teach form-meaning mapping
every structure should trigger a reading action
grammar is not only rule explanation, but processing training

Vocabulary Acquisition Through Reading and Repetition
Principles:

vocabulary grows through recognition, recurrence, word families, and review
Anki cards convert knowledge into retrievable memory
false friends and function words require repeated exposure

Self-Tested Design
Principles:

the editor is the first learner
no chapter becomes stable before self-testing
failed cards and failed self-tests revise the chapter
public method comes after self-verification

Reliability Standard
Every chapter must answer:

What reading ability does this chapter train?
Which mature textbook tradition supports this sequence?
Which SLA principle supports this training action?
What observable learner behavior will show success?
What failure would falsify or weaken this chapter?
What cards should be created?
What self-test checks the chapter?
How will the Diagnostic Tutor classify failure?

Scientific Temper
The system must remain falsifiable.
If a chapter does not improve recognition, parsing, or reading confidence, it must be revised.
If a card is too vague to review, it must be split or deleted.
If a self-test does not expose a gap, it must be rewritten.
If a Proust-oriented example is too difficult for the stage, it must be simplified.
Core Rule
No chapter becomes stable until it has been self-tested by the editor.

AGENT-Review-Rubric.title: AGENT-Review-Rubric
AGENT-Review-Rubric.content:
Agent Review Rubric
Use this rubric for Language Training reviews.
Alignment

Language Training remains part of Proustian.
French remains the language precision layer.
Translation Training is integrated but not confused with French Reading Textbook.
The system supports Proust source-text access, Pattern Cards, terms, syntax, and the course evidence chain.

Content-First Check

No homepage work.
No CSS work.
No Quartz config work.
No visual polish.
No separate repository.

French Reading Textbook Check

A0-to-B1 progression is visible.
English scaffold is clear.
French is the target language.
Essential reading grammar is preserved.
Irrelevant general French is avoided where possible.
Proust direction is present without fake A0 depth.
The chapter follows a recognized reading-language sequence.
The chapter trains one observable reading action.
Morphology and syntax are explicit when needed.
The chapter distinguishes form, function, and meaning.
The chapter includes card-conversion potential.

Pedagogical Reliability Check

The chapter names its source tradition or pedagogical basis.
The learning target is clear and observable.
The self-test can expose a real gap.
Failure can revise the chapter, cards, or self-test.
The Diagnostic Tutor can classify likely failure.
The editor has self-tested the chapter before it is marked stable.

Skill Compliance

Did the chapter invoke the relevant skills?
Are outputs compatible with the required skill formats?
Are card targets reviewable?
Are failure signals visible?
Is Proustian alignment specific?
Did vocabulary work use the correct vocabulary skill rather than a generic list?
Did the diagnostic step classify failure instead of prescribing blanket repetition?

Translation Training Check

Chinese and English may both be used.
The track trains paraphrase, transfer, rewriting, and expression.
It does not merge into French textbook chapters.

Verdicts

Pass: ready to use.
Revise: targeted fixes required.
Reject: do not continue until repaired.

No chapter may receive Pass if it is not auditable under Pedagogical Audit Principles.

AGENT-Workflow.title: AGENT-Workflow
AGENT-Workflow.content:
Agent Workflow
Core Rule
Only the Builder / Integrator may modify files.
All other agents must return review notes, designs, or correction proposals.
Standard Workflow

Textbook Architect drafts or reviews chapter structure and source tradition.
Vocabulary Architect checks vocabulary progression and card-conversion potential.
French Grammar Examiner checks form, function, meaning, and syntax.
Anki Card Architect converts knowledge points into reviewable cards.
Diagnostic Tutor checks whether likely failures can be classified.
Translation Training Designer maintains translation exercises and cards.
The editor self-tests the chapter, cards, and self-test.
Final Examiner gives Pass / Revise / Reject.
Builder / Integrator applies approved revisions.

Pedagogical Audit Step
Every chapter must pass the audit in Pedagogical Audit Principles before it is considered stable.
The audit asks:

What does this chapter train?
Why this sequence?
What textbook or SLA principle supports it?
What evidence shows learning?
What failure revises it?
What cards preserve it?
What diagnostic category repairs it?

Skill-Gated Chapter Acceptance
Before a chapter is accepted:

Draft using SKILL-Chapter-Design.
Audit using SKILL-Pedagogical-Audit.
Check vocabulary using relevant vocabulary skills: SKILL-Cognate-Mapping, SKILL-False-Friend-Alert, or SKILL-Function-Word-Control.
Convert knowledge using SKILL-Card-Conversion.
Diagnose test failures using SKILL-Gap-Diagnosis.
Check target fit using SKILL-Proustian-Alignment.

Review Verdicts

Pass: usable as-is.
Revise: usable after targeted correction.
Reject: do not continue until repaired.

Anti-Drift Rules
Do not:

turn French Reading Textbook into a generic French course
turn Translation Training into French grammar
use Chinese as scaffold in French textbook
make workbook-style dead drills the center
beautify before content
touch homepage or CSS
create a second repository

CARD-Policy.title: CARD-Policy
CARD-Policy.content:
Card Policy
Cards repeat what the textbook has already taught.
Cards do not teach new grammar by themselves.
Good cards are small, answerable, and tied to reading.
Cards are the retrieval engine of the textbook. They convert chapter knowledge into reviewable memory.
One card should test one knowledge point.
Avoid:

large translation prompts
literary interpretation cards
cards with multiple possible answers
cards that require grammar not yet introduced

Use cards for:

forms
articles
gender and number
function words
false friends
sentence skeletons
Proust-oriented micro-patterns

Reliability Rules

If a card is too vague to review, split it or delete it.
If a card tests appreciation rather than recall, recognition, form, function, or parsing, rewrite it.
If a card fails repeatedly, diagnose whether the issue is the card, the chapter, or the learner’s retrieval gap.
Cloze cards should be used only where deletion helps retrieval.

LTF-Chapter-001-Cognates-and-Reading-Con.content:
Chapter 001 — Recognizing French on the Page
Subtitle: Cognates and Reading Confidence
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to recognize that a zero-beginner is not starting from nothing. Many French literary and academic words resemble English words closely enough to give the reader an initial foothold.
2. Reading Problem
The first danger is panic. A French page can look opaque before the reader has learned to notice what is already partly visible.
The second danger is overconfidence. Recognition is not mastery. A familiar-looking word gives a hypothesis, not a final interpretation.
3. Core Knowledge
A cognate is a word that resembles a word in another language because of shared history or borrowing.
For English readers, many French abstract nouns are visually recognizable: mémoire, sensation, perception, forme, and impression.
This resemblance helps the reader begin. It does not remove the need to check grammar, sentence position, modifiers, and context.
The first reading action is controlled recognition:

Notice the familiar shape.
Propose a basic English support word.
Mark uncertainty.
Continue reading the sentence.

4. Vocabulary
4.1 Recognition Vocabulary






































































FrenchEnglish supportFirst cautionmémoirememoryMay mean memory as faculty, record, or recollection.sensationsensationContext decides force.impressionimpressionCan be mental, sensory, or artistic.attentionattentionOften tied to perception and judgment.perceptionperceptionAbstract but useful.imageimageMay be visual, mental, or literary.formeformCan mean shape, form, or artistic form.possiblepossibleHigh-confidence cognate.visiblevisibleHigh-confidence cognate.naturenatureMeaning depends on context.silencesilenceHigh-confidence cognate.momentmomentHigh-confidence cognate.
4.2 New Core Vocabulary

mémoire: memory
sensation: sensation
impression: impression
attention: attention
forme: form
image: image

4.3 Function Words
No new function words are required yet.
Do not skip articles when they appear. In later chapters, le, la, un, and une will become structural signals.
4.4 Proust Direction
Proust is difficult not because every word is opaque, but because recognizable words are arranged, delayed, modified, and transformed inside long French sentences.
4.5 Card Targets

cognate recognition
English support word
recognition versus mastery
Proust-direction warning

5. Forms and Patterns

























PatternExampleReading value-tionsensation, attention, perceptionOften resembles English -tion.final -eforme, imageOften silent; do not treat it as an English ending.accent markmémoireThe accent changes French spelling and sound, but the visual family may remain recognizable.
6. Model Sentences
These are controlled training sentences, not Proust quotations.

La mémoire.
Une sensation.
Une impression visible.
La forme possible.
Le silence.

7. Reading Method
Use a three-step recognition method:

Mark the recognizable word.
Give an English support word.
Add a question mark if meaning may shift in context.

Example:
mémoire → memory → check whether the sentence means personal memory, faculty of memory, or a record.
8. Proustian Alignment
This chapter supports U1’s method: do not rush from recognition to interpretation. A recognizable word is an entrance. It must still return to the sentence and to the passage.
9. Self-Test Link

Self-Test Chapter 001

10. Card Targets

Chapter 001 Cards
mémoire
sensation
impression
attention
recognition is not mastery

11. Diagnostic Notes
If the reader guesses too broadly from English resemblance, assign false-friend repair in Chapter 002.
If the reader cannot identify any familiar forms, review the recognition vocabulary before adding new words.

Chapter 002 — When English Misleads
Subtitle: False Friends and Controlled Guessing
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to use French-English resemblance carefully. Cognates help reading, but some familiar-looking words mislead.
2. Reading Problem
After Chapter 001, the reader may begin to trust visual resemblance too much. This produces fast but false interpretations.
The problem is not guessing. The problem is uncontrolled guessing.
3. Core Knowledge
A false friend is a word that resembles an English word but does not share its expected meaning.
A partial cognate is a word that overlaps with English in some contexts but shifts in others.
Controlled guessing means:

Notice resemblance.
Propose a possible meaning.
Check against sentence context.
Refuse the guess if it does not fit.

4. Vocabulary
4.1 Recognition Vocabulary








































FrenchMisleading English expectationControlled reading valueactuellementactuallycurrently / at presentattendreattendto wait forignorerignorenot to know / to be unaware ofsensiblesensiblesensitive / perceptibleéventuellementeventuallypossibly / if necessarylibrairielibrarybookstore
4.2 New Core Vocabulary

actuellement: currently
attendre: to wait for
ignorer: not to know
sensible: sensitive / perceptible
éventuellement: possibly
librairie: bookstore

4.3 Function Words
No new function words are required yet.
Watch for context words around false friends. They often reveal whether the English guess is wrong.
4.4 Proust Direction
The reader must learn to use resemblance without surrendering judgment. Proustian reading requires inference, but every inference must remain testable.
4.5 Card Targets

false friend recognition
correction of English expectation
controlled guessing steps
error-correction cards

5. Forms and Patterns






























TypeExampleRiskadverbactuellementLooks like “actually.”verbattendreLooks like “attend.”adjectivesensibleLooks like “sensible.”nounlibrairieLooks like “library.”
6. Model Sentences
These are controlled training sentences.

Actuellement, le lecteur attend.
Le narrateur ignore une sensation.
Une impression sensible apparaît.
Éventuellement, une image revient.
La librairie n’est pas une bibliothèque.

7. Reading Method
Use the false-friend check:

Does the word look familiar?
Is it a known false friend?
Does the English guess fit the sentence?
What safer reading value should replace it?

8. Proustian Alignment
This chapter supports U1’s claim/problem method. A first claim about a word may be wrong. The reader must test it, expose its limit, and return to the sentence.

If the reader repeatedly translates by visual resemblance alone, assign error-correction cards before continuing.
If the reader becomes afraid to guess, review Chapter 001: the goal is controlled confidence, not avoidance.

Chapter 003 — Word Families
Subtitle: Suffixes, Prefixes, and Recognition Patterns
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to recognize word families instead of memorizing isolated words.
2. Reading Problem
French reading becomes slow if every word is treated as new. The reader needs pattern recognition: suffixes, prefixes, and historical spelling clues.
3. Core Knowledge
A word family is a group of related forms that share a root or pattern.
For reading, the goal is not full etymology. The goal is fast, cautious recognition.
Patterns such as -tion, -ité, and -ment help the reader identify abstract nouns and adverbs. Endings such as -able, -ible, -if, and -ive help the reader recognize adjectives. A circumflex may mark a historical lost s, as in forêt and forest.
4. Vocabulary

mouvement: movement
actif: active, masculine
active: active, feminine
étude: study
forêt: forest

4.3 Function Words
No new function words are required yet.
4.4 Proust Direction
Proustian reading requires the ability to recognize families of abstraction, perception, and movement.
4.5 Card Targets

suffix recognition
prefix recognition
circumflex as spelling clue
word family grouping

5. Forms and Patterns













































PatternCommon reading signalExamples-tionabstract action or stateattention, sensation, perception-itéabstract qualitysensibilité-mentnoun or adverb patternmouvement-able / -iblepossibility or capacityvisible, possible-if / -iveadjective pairactif / activeé- / es-historical relation clueétude / studycircumflexpossible lost s clueforêt / forest
6. Model Sentences
These are controlled training sentences.

Une sensation visible.
Une forme possible.
La sensibilité.
Le mouvement de la mémoire.
Une image active.

7. Reading Method
Use the family recognition method:

Identify the ending or spelling clue.
Connect it to a known pattern.
Propose an English support word.
Check whether the sentence confirms it.

8. Proustian Alignment
U1 asks the reader to move from a single cliché to multiple testable paths. Word families make those paths visible: memory, sensation, perception, image, form, and movement become repeatable lexical fields.

If the reader memorizes isolated words but misses patterns, assign suffix recognition cards.
If the reader overgeneralizes patterns, return to Chapter 002 and controlled guessing.

Chapter 004 — Function Words I
Subtitle: Small Words That Control Reading
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to treat small French words as structural controls, not background noise.
2. Reading Problem
Beginners often look for nouns and ignore small words. In French reading, this fails quickly. Function words tell the reader how sentence parts attach.
3. Core Knowledge
Function words are small, frequent words that express relation, location, addition, contrast, comparison, presence, or absence.
They may carry less obvious dictionary meaning than nouns, but they control reading.
The first rule: do not skip small words.
4. Vocabulary
4.1 Recognition Vocabulary























































FrenchFirst reading valueReading actiondeof / from / relationMark relation.àto / at / relationMark direction or location.etandMark addition.maisbutMark contrast.dansin / insideMark location or frame.suron / uponMark position or topic pressure.avecwithMark accompaniment.sanswithoutMark absence.commeas / likeMark comparison.
4.2 New Core Vocabulary

à
et
mais
dans
sur
avec
sans
comme

4.3 Function Words
This chapter is entirely about function words.
4.4 Proust Direction
Long French sentences are held together by relation words. Function words tell the reader how parts of a sentence attach to one another.
4.5 Card Targets

one function word per card
basic relation value
controlled micro-sentence
attachment question

5. Forms and Patterns



































FunctionWordsBasic questionRelationde, àWhat is connected to what?Addition / contrastet, maisIs the sentence adding or turning?Location / framedans, surWhere is the word or idea placed?Presence / absenceavec, sansWhat is present or missing?ComparisoncommeWhat is being compared?
6. Model Sentences
These are controlled training sentences.

La mémoire de la sensation.
Une image dans la mémoire.
Le silence et l’attention.
Une impression sans forme.
Une sensation comme une image.

7. Reading Method
Use the function-word marking method:

Mark every small word.
Name its first function.
Ask what it attaches.
Continue before interpreting.

8. Proustian Alignment
U1’s textual return depends on attachment. A theory may fly outward, but the sentence is held together by small relation words. Function words are the grammar of return.

If the reader skips small words, assign function-word recognition cards.

Chapter 005 — What Is a French Sentence?
Subtitle: Subject, Verb, Complement, Modifier
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to identify the basic structure of a French sentence before interpretation.
2. Reading Problem
The reader may now recognize words, patterns, and function words, but recognition alone does not produce sentence reading. The sentence must be seen as a structure.
3. Core Knowledge
A controlled French sentence usually contains:

a subject
a conjugated verb
sometimes a complement
sometimes a modifier

The subject names what the sentence is about. The conjugated verb carries the main movement. The complement completes the verb or thought. The modifier adds circumstance, quality, place, time, or relation.
4. Vocabulary
4.1 Recognition Vocabulary









































FrenchReading valuele souvenirthe memory / recollectionla chambrethe roomsilencieusesilent, feminineune sensationa sensationle tempstimel’impressionthe impressionla mémoirememoryune imagean image
4.2 New Core Vocabulary

souvenir: memory / recollection
revient: returns / comes back
semble: seems
silencieuse: silent, feminine
apparaît: appears
transforme: transforms

4.3 Function Words

dans: in / inside

4.4 Proust Direction
Even the longest Proustian sentence is built from grammatical relations. The reader must learn to see structure before interpretation.
4.5 Card Targets

subject
conjugated verb
complement
modifier
sentence before interpretation

5. Forms and Patterns






























TermReading questionExampleSubjectWho or what is the sentence about?Le souvenirVerbWhat form carries the movement?revientComplementWhat completes the verb or thought?l’impressionModifierWhat adds place, quality, or circumstance?Dans la mémoire
Basic pattern:
Subject + conjugated verb + complement / modifier
6. Model Sentences

Le souvenir revient.
La chambre semble silencieuse.
Une sensation apparaît.
Le temps transforme l’impression.
Dans la mémoire, une image revient.

7. Reading Method
Use the sentence-seeing method:

Find the full sentence.
Find the subject.
Find the conjugated verb.
Ask whether there is a complement.
Mark any modifier.
Give a plain English structural control.
Interpret only after the structure is visible.

8. Proustian Alignment
This chapter completes the first Stage 0 arc. U1 teaches textual return as a method. Chapter 005 makes textual return grammatical: every claim must come back to the sentence.
9. Self-Test Link

10. Card Targets

Chapter 005 Cards
subject recognition
verb recognition
complement recognition
modifier recognition
English structural control

11. Diagnostic Notes
If the reader recognizes vocabulary but cannot parse the sentence, assign parsing cards.
If the reader translates before structure is visible, return to the sentence-seeing method.

Literature-Importance-Ranking-V0.1.title: Literature Importance Ranking V0.1
Literature-Importance-Ranking-V0.1.content:
Literature Importance Ranking V0.1
This ranking keeps Proust at the center while sorting supporting literature by use, timing, and evidence value.
Level 1｜Core Field

Marcel Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu

Use:
The central field of reading, evidence, scenes, problems, and aesthetic truth.
Why it matters:
Every method lens, bridge text, and expansion node must return to Proust rather than replacing him as the center.
When to read:
Continuously, scene by scene, with attention to signs, sensory experience, time, misrecognition, and form.
NotebookLM first?
Yes. This is the primary evidence base and should enter NotebookLM before any secondary structure becomes public.
Level 2｜Primary Method Lenses

Gilles Deleuze, Proust and Signs
Gérard Genette, Narrative Discourse
Joshua Landy, Philosophy as Fiction
Jean-Jacques Nattiez, Proust as Musician
Vladimir Jankélévitch, Music and the Ineffable
Mieke Bal, The Mottled Screen
Jonathan Crary, Suspensions of Perception
Alain Corbin, The Foul and the Fragrant
Alain Corbin, Village Bells

Use:
Provide the first working lenses for signs, narrative time, philosophical fiction, music, visual attention, and sensory history.
Why it matters:
These sources turn peripheral entry points into precise routes back toward Proust.
When to read:
After identifying a Proustian scene or question, then again when shaping verified question blocks.
NotebookLM first?
Yes, after Proust. These sources should be uploaded early as method anchors for evidence checking.
Level 3｜Disciplinary Anchors

Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Eye and Mind
T. J. Clark, The Painting of Modern Life
Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation
Fernand Braudel, On History
Marc Bloch, The Historian’s Craft
Lucien Febvre, A New Kind of History
Jacques Le Goff, History and Memory
The Cambridge Companion to Proust
Proust and the Arts
Proust and the Visual

Use:
Stabilize claims across perception, visual modernity, music, historical method, memory, and Proust studies.
Why it matters:
They prevent the reading garden from becoming only associative by giving each axis disciplinary weight.
When to read:
When a reading path needs stronger conceptual support or when a public page risks overextension.
NotebookLM first?
Selective yes. Upload by packet need, especially for visuality, music, and historical evidence questions.
Level 4｜Orientation / Bridge Texts

Adam Watt, The Cambridge Introduction to Marcel Proust
Roger Shattuck, Proust’s Way
David Ellison, A Reader’s Guide to Proust’s In Search of Lost Time
Eric Karpeles, Paintings in Proust
Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, The Weather in Proust

Use:
Offer orientation, scene access, and bridge language between close reading and public-facing explanation.
Why it matters:
These texts help visitors enter Proust without flattening the project into summary.
When to read:
Before drafting public-facing pages or when a packet needs a clean bridge from question to passage.
NotebookLM first?
Yes for bridge support, but after Proust and the primary method lenses.
Level 5｜Expansion Nodes

Adorno
Schoenberg
Rosen
Thomas Mann, Doctor Faustus
Warburg
Lévi-Strauss
Didi-Huberman
Sara Danius, The Senses of Modernism
Shattuck, The Banquet Years

Use:
Expand specific constellations around modernism, music, image memory, myth, sensory modernity, and artistic form.
Why it matters:
They widen the field without becoming the main architecture of the site.
When to read:
Only after a Proustian question has become stable and needs a wider comparative horizon.
NotebookLM first?
No, except for targeted packets where a verified expansion would clarify an existing Proust-centered question.
Level 6｜Not Now / Archive

broad biography
full music history surveys
full art history surveys
broad poststructuralist expansion
large Zotero evidence-chain work
database-heavy website features

Use:
Hold useful but currently distracting directions outside the first public reading structure.
Why it matters:
The project needs density before scale, and public pages should not be pulled into archive management or encyclopedic coverage.
When to read:
Later, only when a specific reading page or packet requires it.
NotebookLM first?
No. These materials should wait until the core evidence packets are stable.

Question-Gradient.title: Question-Gradient
Question-Gradient.content:
Question Gradient
Root Question
How does Proust train the reader to discover truth through signs, sensation, attention, misrecognition, and artistic form?
Starting Questions

What sign appears before it is understood?
What kind of sensation starts the reading process?
What kind of delay, mistake, or misrecognition organizes the scene?
What secondary lens clarifies the passage without replacing Proust?
What form of attention does the passage train?
How can this passage become a reader-facing card?

U1｜Signs / Method
How does Proust train the reader to read signs rather than merely follow plot, psychology, or memory?
Method entrance:

U1 General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading

Supporting questions:

What forces thought before interpretation begins?
What makes a sign readable?
How does Deleuze help without replacing Proust?

U2｜Memory / Time / Space
How does Proust transform memory from recollection into a structure of signs, time, space, and artistic discovery?
Supporting questions:

How does the Madeleine scene turn sensation into discovery?
How does involuntary memory reopen time through place and sensation?
How does habit shape what can or cannot be perceived?

U3｜Music / Ineffable
How does Vinteuil’s music move from emotional sign to artistic truth, ineffable experience, and novelistic structure?
Supporting questions:

How does music carry truth before it can be explained?
How does the little phrase move from love sign to art sign?
What does the ineffable allow the novel to think?

U4｜Visuality / Gaze / Photography / Attention
How does Proust transform seeing into a discipline of attention, misrecognition, capture, and artistic truth?
Supporting questions:

How does the Vermeer yellow wall become a test of attention?
How does seeing differ from understanding?
How do gaze, framing, and capture organize misrecognition?

U5｜Space / Sensory History
How do spaces and sensory environments in Proust produce social time and historical subjectivity?
Supporting questions:

How do rooms and salons become social machines?
How do bells gather collective time?
How do smell and atmosphere mark social boundaries?

U6｜Writing Apparatus
How can U1–U5 be transformed into teachable, writable, reader-facing forms without losing aesthetic and intellectual force?
Supporting questions:

How does a Passage Card become a reader-facing block?
How does a Unit Digest become a course page?
How does the website remain a reading garden rather than a content dump?

U6 — Writing Apparatus
How can reading, passage cards, language training, and conceptual transfer become teachable, writable, reader-facing forms?

U1-General-Introduction-Memory-Cliche-to.title: U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
U1-General-Introduction-Memory-Cliche-to.content:
U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
U1 is not a signs unit. It is the general introduction that uses the memory cliché as a methodological hinge: from involuntary memory to competing reading lenses, from single-center interpretation to claim/problem chains, and finally back to Proust’s textual world.
Position｜U1 as General Introduction
U1 establishes the course’s methodological tendency. It does not ask the reader to replace memory with signs, nor to choose Deleuze as the master key. It shows how the cliché “Proust is a novelist of memory” becomes the first pressure point from which the whole course opens.
Not This｜Signs as Course Center
U1 should not make “signs” into a new sovereign center. Deleuze remains useful, but he is only one theoretical line among several.
But This｜Memory Cliché as Methodological Hinge
The course begins with the force and insufficiency of involuntary memory, then unfolds multiple reading paths that return to the novel.

Core formulation: U1 is a methodological overture. It explains how Proustian 2.0 reads through strong theoretical positions without allowing any one of them to own Proust.

The Memory Cliché as Starting Pressure
The tradition of involuntary memory is not a weak opponent. It is powerful enough to become a recurring object of criticism, compression, displacement, and renewal. U1 must therefore begin by granting its force before showing why it cannot remain the only center.
English Claim
Memory is powerful but insufficient.
Proust is often entered through lost time, involuntary memory, and the return of the personal past. This entry is legitimate, but incomplete. If memory becomes the first and final explanation, the novel’s errors, delays, social codes, musical pressures, visual fragments, and artistic discoveries are flattened.
中文判断
记忆是强传统，但不是最终中心。
非自愿记忆当然构成《追忆》中最具震动性的经验之一。但如果它成为唯一解释，小说中的误读、延宕、社交姿态、爱情迷误、音乐压力、视觉凝聚与艺术真理都会被压成“过去回来了”。

U1 does not reject memory. It uses memory as the first hinge through which Proustian reading moves from a single strong tradition toward a polycentric method.

Basic Literature Review as Method
The literature review in U1 should not be a bibliography dump. It should present reading positions: what each lens sees, what it risks, and how it returns to the Proustian text-world.









































Reading PositionWhat It SeesWhat It RisksReturn to TextMemory TraditionLost time returns through sensation, involuntary memory, and the sudden recovery of personal history.Reducing the novel to recollection, nostalgia, or psychological recovery.Ask what returns, and why the return is delayed, unstable, or transformed.DeleuzeSigns force thought; the narrator learns through error, apprenticeship, and interpretation.Flattening prose into taxonomy or turning Proust into Deleuze.Ask whether signs clarify the passage, or whether classification weakens its literary pressure.PouletMemory becomes space; moments and places condense into fields of vision.Freezing narrative movement into static contemplation.Ask what spatial image or mosaic-like arrangement the passage forms.Narrative DiscourseMeaning emerges through delay, order, duration, frequency, voice, retrospection, and narrative arrangement.Over-formalizing the text and losing the pressure of experience.Ask how the passage becomes readable only through narrative structure.Visual / Music / Sensory PathsProust transforms image, sound, smell, gesture, and atmosphere into literary form.Drifting into art history, musicology, or sensory history without textual return.Ask how the medium is absorbed by the novel rather than simply added to it.
Polycentric Reading｜No Center Does Not Mean No Judgment
U1 introduces a polycentric method. “No center” does not mean arbitrary wandering. It means no single theory is allowed to become sovereign. Each lens must become strong enough to make a claim, produce a problem, and submit itself to textual testing.
Rule 1｜No single theory owns Proust.
Memory, signs, space, narrative delay, music, visuality, and sensory history are all possible entrances, not final masters.
Rule 2｜Every lens must become strong.
A weak lens produces decoration. A strong lens produces a claim, a problem, and a pressure against other readings.
Rule 3｜The text tests every claim.
A theory is useful only when it returns to a sentence, scene, rhythm, object, gesture, sound, or misrecognition.
Claim / Problem Chain
This is the central writing method for U1. The goal is not to list themes, but to unfold claims until their problems, counterclaims, limits, and textual returns become visible.








































StepActionFunction1ClaimState what a reading position asserts.2PassageAttach the claim to a concrete Proust scene.3ProblemShow what the claim cannot easily explain.4Counter-ClaimLet another lens answer or resist it.5LimitExpose where the second lens also begins to fail.6ReturnGo back to the prose and form a judgment.

Method principle: The more fully a claim/problem chain is unfolded, the more testable, comparable, and recoverable the reading becomes. This is U1’s version of rigor.

Kite-Line Reading｜Textual Spine and Theoretical Lines
The hand-drawn model becomes the course’s visual method: theory flies outward from the text, reaches its horizon, dissolves, and returns.
English Formulation
The text is the spine.
Theories are lines released above it. Each line may fly outward, rise, diverge, and open a new field of vision. But every line must return to the Proustian text-world.
中文表述
文本是脊骨。
理论是在文本脊骨上方放飞的线束。每条理论线都可以飞出、分叉、升高，但最终必须重新降落到普鲁斯特的句子、场景、感官与叙事运动之中。

Proustian 2.0 does not reject theory. It releases theory from the text, lets it fly to its horizon, watches it dissolve, and then returns to the novel and to the reader’s own perception.

Reading Action｜U1 Trains Method, Not Sign Classification
The reading action no longer begins by asking “what kind of sign is this?” It begins with the passage and asks what pressure appears. Signs are one possible lens, not the center.

Start with a Proust passage, not a theory.
Identify the dominant pressure: memory, error, delay, image, sound, social gesture, sensation, or artistic form.
Choose one provisional lens: memory, signs, space, narrative discourse, visuality, music, or sensory history.
Ask what this lens makes visible in the passage.
Ask what this lens fails to see, weakens, or over-systematizes.
Let another lens answer, resist, or intensify the first claim.
Return to the prose: sentence, rhythm, scene, gesture, object, sound, or image.
Produce a readerly judgment: what did this passage teach the reader to see?

Core Lenses Opened by U1
U1 introduces several strong reading lenses. Each one is provisional. Each one must return to the passage.
Memory

What lost past returns?
What sensory shock triggers it?
Why is return not enough?

Signs

What pressure forces interpretation?
What does the narrator misread?
Where does apprenticeship begin?

Space / Vision

What spatial image forms?
How do moments and places become a mosaic?
What does vision compress?

Narrative Discourse

What is delayed?
Who knows what, and when?
How does narrative order make meaning possible?

Music / Visuality

How does another art enter the novel?
Does the novel imitate it or transform it?
What new form of truth appears?

Sensory / Social Space

How do smell, sound, room, salon, or street produce social time?
What historical pressure enters private experience?

Scene Anchors as Test Cases
These are not proof examples for a single theory. They are testing grounds where multiple lenses compete and return.
Madeleine
Memory, sensation, sign, habit, delay, and narrative reorganization.
Swann / Odette
Love, jealousy, deception, interpretation, social signs, and misreading.
Names of Places
Fantasy, expectation, disappointment, space, language, and desire.
Vinteuil
Music, love, ineffable truth, repetition, and artistic transformation.
Vermeer
Visual attention, art sign, mortality, color, detail, and judgment.
Transition to U2–U6
U1 opens the whole course. It does not close itself around Deleuze or signs. Its output is a method that can move into later units.








































Question Opened in U1Later UnitCourse FunctionWhy is memory powerful but insufficient?U2｜Memory / Time / SpaceTurns recollection into structure, delay, space, and passage-level reading.How do signs, errors, and forced thought train the reader?U1 bridge + U2Provides a portable method without making Deleuze the center.How does music become a path toward truth?U3｜Music / IneffableMoves from emotional motif to artistic and novelistic structure.How does seeing become attention and judgment?U4｜Visuality / GazeReads visual fragments as pressures on perception and form.How do spaces and sensations produce social time?U5｜Sensory History / Social SpaceLinks private sensation with historical and social form.How can reading become a reader-facing structure?U6｜Writing ApparatusConverts U1–U5 into pages, cards, labs, and course architecture.
Final Judgment
The center is not memory, not signs, not Deleuze, not Poulet, and not any single theory. The center is the disciplined effort to approach Proust’s novel through competing, testable, returnable reading paths.

Chapter 001 — What Is a French Sentence?
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to see a French sentence as an ordered unit before interpretation.
At this level, a controlled French sentence usually gives:

a subject group
a conjugated verb
sometimes, a completion

The first task is not literary interpretation. The first task is structural sight.
2. Proustian Reading Target
Proust remains the final target, but Chapter 001 is not direct Proust reading.
This chapter trains the first habit needed for Proust: pause before interpreting, locate the sentence, and identify its main movement.
3. Core Grammar
A French sentence begins with a capital letter and usually ends with a period, question mark, or exclamation mark.
In a very simple sentence, the subject group normally comes before the conjugated verb.
Controlled pattern for this chapter:
Subject group + conjugated verb + completion, if there is one

Form Card
Prompt: identify a form.

Article + Noun Card
Prompt: identify gender and number.
Example: la chambre
Answer: feminine singular; the room.
Function Word Card
Prompt: give the structural role.

Pattern Card
Prompt: parse a micro-sentence.

Gap Taxonomy
Sentence Visibility
The reader cannot identify the full sentence.
Subject / Verb
The reader cannot locate the subject group or conjugated verb.
Forms
The reader does not recognize tense, person, number, gender, or article.
Function Words
The reader misses a structural word such as de, à, que, or qui.
Word Order
The reader cannot track basic order or delayed material.
English Control
The reader cannot produce a plain English structural check.
Proustian Entry
The reader over-interprets before parsing.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.title: Corpus-Principles
_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Corpus Principles
The course should use Proust as its source horizon from the beginning.
Use:

Proust-oriented vocabulary
Proust-oriented model sentences
short adapted fragments
controlled sentences modeled on Proustian syntax
later, carefully selected source passages

Avoid:

unrelated everyday French
long quotations in early chapters
literary essay commentary in grammar chapters
vocabulary that does not prepare the reader for Proust

Source-status labels:

attested: directly present in the source passage being used.
adapted: shortened or adjusted from source material for teaching.
Proust-oriented: selected because it prepares Proust reading, but not claimed as a quotation.
course-control: supplied by the course for controlled practice.

Early chapters may use simple controlled sentences. Later chapters should increasingly return to authentic Proustian phrases, clauses, and periods.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.title: Pedagogical-Model
_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Pedagogical Model
The model follows the structural discipline of Learn to Read Latin and Learn to Read Greek, adapted for a zero-beginner reader learning to read French toward Proust.
Each chapter should contain:

a precise aim
a reading target
a grammar sequence
forms or paradigms
vocabulary
model sentences
guided parsing
workbook drills
an answer key
cumulative review

The method is reading-first. The reader learns forms and syntax because they make French sentence structure visible.
Language hierarchy:

French is the target language and final textual object.
English is the scaffold language, explanation language, comparison language, and structural control language.
Chinese is reserved for private editor notes only.

Translation is a tool, not the endpoint. English control readings should clarify French structure; they should not turn the workbook into translation training.
The endpoint is controlled reading: seeing the sentence, locating its structure, and eventually following the movement of memory, perception, and delay in Proust.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.title: Project-Statement
_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Project Statement
Learn to Read Proust is a private self-study French reading course.
Its final and only target text is Marcel Proust, A la recherche du temps perdu.
The project is organized as a rigorous textbook + workbook + answer-key system. It is not a general French course, not a conversation course, and not a survey of French literature.
Every chapter should train one reading skill that later becomes necessary for reading Proust with control: sentence recognition, forms, vocabulary, parsing, syntax, memory structures, subordination, and long-period reading.
The course should remain cumulative. New grammar should be introduced in sequence, practiced in drills, checked in the answer key, and reviewed later.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.title: Course-Prospectus
_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Course Prospectus
Learn to Read Proust is a self-study French reading course for a zero-beginner whose final target is Marcel Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu.
The course is not a general French course. It is also not a translation workbook or a literary essay project.
The course trains the reader to see French sentence structure before interpretation. Proust remains the final textual object, but early lessons must stay pedagogically flexible and structurally clear.
Book I begins with the simplest reading acts: finding the sentence, identifying the subject and verb, recognizing nouns and articles, and using English as a structural control language.
The course should be rigorous, cumulative, and workbook-driven.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.title: Proust-Target-Policy
_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Proust Target Policy
The final target is Marcel Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu, in French.
Early chapters do not need to read Proust directly. They should prepare the reader for Proust by training structural sight.
Use Proust-oriented vocabulary when it helps:

memory
time
room
sensation
perception
sentence movement
narrator as a course-control label

Do not force fake Proustian depth into A0 lessons.
Model sentences may be controlled or adapted. They must be clearly marked as training sentences when they are not quotations.
Long Proust quotations should wait until the reader has enough grammar to parse them.

_archive-language-training/private-legac.content:
Chapter 001 — What Is a French Sentence?
1. Chapter Aim
Learn to see a French sentence as an ordered unit before interpretation.
At this level, a controlled French sentence usually gives:

a subject group
a conjugated verb
sometimes, a completion

The first task is not literary interpretation. The first task is structural sight.
2. Proustian Reading Target
Proust remains the final target, but Chapter 001 is not direct Proust reading.
This chapter trains the first habit needed for Proust: pause before interpreting, locate the sentence, and identify its main movement.
3. Core Grammar
A French sentence begins with a capital letter and usually ends with a period, question mark, or exclamation mark.
In a very simple sentence, the subject group normally comes before the conjugated verb.
Controlled pattern for this chapter:
Subject group + conjugated verb + completion, if there is one
Key terms:

























TermWorking meaning for Chapter 001sentencea complete written unitsubject groupwho or what the sentence is aboutconjugated verbthe verb form that carries the sentence movementcompletiona temporary reading label for a word or group that completes the thought
Some simple training sentences have no completion.
Do not translate too quickly. First locate the structure.
4. Forms / Paradigm
For now, recognize only these present-tense forms.

Note: regarde is used here as a controlled no-object form for recognition. Later chapters will add ordinary object patterns such as “looks at something.”
